narrative: During the 1940s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in traditional practices and cultural identity. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth of kinky hair, was likely worn by many women during this time period. Cornrows, a style of three-strand braids close to the scalp, were also popular and considered a traditional African practice. While there is limited documentation on hairstyles specifically from this era, it is clear that protective styles such as cornrows and perhaps box braids would have been favored due to their ability to minimize manipulation and exposure to environmental elements. The natural texture of kinky hair was likely celebrated and preserved through these styles, which were not only aesthetically pleasing but also served a practical purpose in maintaining hair health. Unfortunately, the source material does not provide more specific information on hairstyles during this decade, but it is evident that Black and African women's hair culture continued to thrive despite the societal pressures of the time.
